title: Joseph Weizenbaum's ELIZA and the First Chatbot (1966)
explainer: In the mid-1960s, MIT researcher Joseph Weizenbaum built ELIZA, a program that used simple pattern-matching and substitution rules - with no real understanding of language - to imitate a Rogerian psychotherapist by reflecting a user's own words back as questions. Weizenbaum was reportedly unsettled that people, including his own secretary, treated the program as if it genuinely understood and cared, a reaction now known as the ELIZA effect. It's a useful caution for 'literacy before craft': fluent, human-sounding output from a language model is not proof that the system understood your prompt or the context behind it.
